Industrial revolution took place in the eighteenth century and rapid growth in science and technology was also observed. text: Unit I: Introduction Physics IX 1.2. INTRODUCTION TO PHYSICS Physics is derived from Greek word 'physikos' meaning the science of natural things. Physics is defined as the study of matter, energy and their mutual interactions. Physics is also considered as the study of the properties of matter, space and time. Physics is further divided into branches to facilitate its study. 1.2.1 Branches of Classical Physics Classical Physics deals with principles developed in many areas of Physics before 20th century and are given below as branches of classical Physics. Each branch of Physics has become so vast that it can be treated as a separate subject. Mechanics It deals with the study of motion of material objects with or without reference of the forces. Heat /Thermal Physics It deals with the nature of heat, mechanisms of heat transfer and its effects on matter. Thermodynamics It deals with conversion of heat energy into other forms of energy (i.e., mechanical, electrical or chemical energy etc.) or vice versa. Optics It deals with the nature, production, propagation of light and phenomena related to it (i.e., reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarization etc.). The

book_title: Balochistan Board Class 9 Physics Textbook (2026 listing)
subject: Physics
text: Optics It deals with the nature, production, propagation of light and phenomena related to it (i.e., reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarization etc.). The working and use of optical instruments such as camera, microscope and telescope etc. is also studied. Electricity and Magnetism / Electromagnetism It deals with the study of the charges which are either at rest or in motion, their effects and their relationship with magnetism. Electromagnetism is the study of phenomena and laws relating electricity and magnetism. Atomic Physics It deals with the study of structure and properties of atoms. Acoustics The branch of Physics that deals with study of sound (i.e., infrasonic, audible sound and ultrasonic), its production, control, propagation, detection and other related phenomena is called acoustics.

text: Unit 1: Introduction Physics IX 1.2.2 Branches of Modern Physics The developments made in 20th century are studied under the heading of "Modern Physics' and its various branches are listed as under. Nuclear Physics: It deals with the study of structure, properties and reactions of nuclei of atoms. Solid State Physics It deals with the study of physical properties of solid materials. It is also called as ‘Condensed Matter Physics'. Semiconductor Physics It deals with study, design and use of devices based on behaviour of electrons in semiconductors. Low Temperature Physics It deals with production of extremely low temperature and study of properties of matter at low temperatures. It is also known as 'Cryogenics' derived from the Greek meaning 'producing cold’. Quantum Mechanics It deals with the study of matter, electromagnetic radiation and their interactions based on quantum theory. Particle Physics It deals with the study of elementary particles of the nucleus. Plasma Physics It deals with the study of production and properties of the ionic state of matter i.e., nuclei without electrons. Plasma is also referred as the fourth state of matter. 1.2.3 Interdisciplinary Fields

Ascientist who specializes in the research of Physics is called Physicist. A further classification is made depending on the area of specialization within physics. 15 HYPOTHESIS, THEORY AND LAW Hypothesis It is defined as the possible explanation of specific observable natural phenomenon based on simplified postulates assumptions or axioms which may be true or untrue. A hypothesis requires further scientific observations and research in order to establish whether the postulates are true or not. The hypothesis may change significantly with more observations. The special theory of relativity is based on two postulates. Bohr model of hydrogen atom is also based on certain postulates. You will study these topics in higher classes. Theory When a hypothesis is tested multiple times with positive results then it is given the name of theory. A theory about a natural phenomenon is more certain than a hypothesis. The

The studies about earthquakes, volcanoes and rocks under sea floor etc. provide evidence about plate tectonic theory. Law A relation among different parameters of a phenomenon which has been found empirically true and applicable in all cases is called a law. text: Length, area, volume, mass, density, time, temperature, speed, force and pressure etc. are examples of physical quantities. A number of physical quantities such as length, mass, time and temperature etc. can be measured directly i.e., they do not depend on other quantities. On the other hand, certain quantities depend on other quantities and cannot be measured directly. Force is defined as the product of mass and acceleration. The measurement of force involves the measurement of two physical quantities i.e., mass and acceleration. Similarly, momentum is defined as the product of mass and velocity. Thus, the measurement of momentum involves the measurement of two quantities namely mass and velocity. Aphysical quantity is represented by a number followed by is proper unit. This number represents the size or magnitude of the physical quantity with a proper unit. The number alone is meaningless. For example, if mass of an object is 10 kilograms, then 10 is anumber that gives the size or magnitude of the quantity while kilogram is the unit of mass. The quantities given above are examples of non-physical quantities. A quantity which cannot be measured and cannot be expressed in terms of standard units is called a non-physical quantity. 2.2 Types of Physical Quantities Physical quantities are classified into following two groups (i) Base quantities and (ii) Derived quantities. 2.2.1 Base Quantities The physical quantities in terms of which other physical quantities can be measured are called base quantities. No measurement is absolutely accurate or precise. There is always an uncertainty in every measurement due to certain causes. The uncertainty in a measurement is termed as error. There are two types of errors in measurements i.e., systematic error and random error. 2.11.1 Systematic Error An error which repeats in the measurement with same magnitude and same sign is called a systematic error. It produces a consistent difference in readings. This error occurs due to the presence of zero error or poor calibration of the instrument. It may be due to the limitations of the method used for measurement of specified quantity. The systematic error can be minimized by comparing the given instrument with a more accurate instrument and making the relevant corrections in the readings. The

For example, the diameter of metallic wire as measured by a micrometer screw gauge is 2.65 mm, then there are three significant figures and the last digit 5 is uncertain or doubtful. Precision refers to how closely two or more measurements of the same quantity agree with one another i.e., diameter of cylinder on present case. Precision can be expressed as the difference between value of an individual measurement of a physical quantity and the value of arithmetic mean for successive or repeated measurements of the same quantity. Thus, Precision = Value of the individual measurement — Value of arithmetic mean It is obvious from above word equation that the greater will be the precision of a measurement if above difference is small. text: la SUMMARY A quantity which can be measured and expressed in terms of standard units is called a physical quantity. A physical quantity can be expressed as a numerical value with an appropriate unit. A quantity which cannot be measured and cannot be expressed in terms of standard units is called a non-physical quantity. Those physical quantities in terms of which other physical quantities can be measured are called base quantities. Those quantities which can be derived from base quantities are known as derived quantities. Derived quantities can be obtained by combination of (i.e., multiplication or division) of two or more than two base quantities. The unit of base quantity is known as base unit. The units ofa derived quantity are known as derived units. Prefixes are the words or letter such as mega, kilo, centi, milli and micro etc. added before SI units ofa physical quantity. In scientific notation the given number is expressed as some power of ten multiplied by a number which lies between | and 10. A quantity which is completely specified by its magnitude only is called a scalar quantity. A quantity which is completely specified by its magnitude as well as direction is called a

If two or more vectors are to be added then they can be replaced by a single vector, called resultant vector, that has the same effect as the combined effect of all the given vectors. Ameasuring instrument is a device used for measuring a physical quantity. Metre rule, measuring tape, Vernier callipers and screw gauge are length measuring instruments. Graduated or measuring cylinder is used to measure the volume ofa liquid. Anerror which repeats in the measurement with same magnitude and same sign is called a systematic error. An error which repeats in the measurement with different magnitude and sign under the same experimental conditions is called a random error. The accurately known digits and the first uncertain or doubtful digit in an expression are called significant figures. text: Unit 3: Kinematics Physics IX 3.8 MOTION UNDER GRAVITY Galileo (1564 - 1642) was the first scientist who showed experimentally that a heavy object and a light object both reach the ground at the same time provided that these are dropped from the same height. He dropped a number of objects of different masses from the leaning tower of Pisa and observed that all objects reached ground at the same time. It may be pointed out that these objects fall on the ground due the gravitational pull of Earth. From this fact, he concluded that if we neglect the air resistance, then all objects whether light or heavy fall on Earth with uniform acceleration. This acceleration is known as gravitational acceleration. This gravitational acceleration is represented by 'g'. Its value near the surface of Earth is 9.8 ms”. text: la o-¢ cree SUMMARY Mechanics is defined as the branch of Physics that deals with the study of forces, motion and their mutual relationship. Mechanics is divided into three parts. (i) Statics (ii) Kinematics (iii) Dynamics The part of mechanics that deals with the study of objects at rest is called statics. The part of mechanics that deals with the study of motion of objects without any reference to the cause of motion is called kinematics. The part of mechanics that deals with the study of motion with the reference of mass and force is called dynamics. A body is said to be at rest if it does not change its position with respect to its surroundings. A body is said to be in motion if it changes its position with respect to its surroundings. Rest and motion are relative terms. Ifa body moves along a line without any vibration or rotation, then its motion said to be translatory motion. If the motion of a body is ina straight line, it is said to have linear motion. Ifa body moves ina circle, then its motion is called circular motion. Ifa body moves in an irregular manner, then its motion is called random motion. When each point of a body moves around a fixed point or axis, then the

When each point of a body moves around a fixed point or axis, then the motion of this body is called rotatory motion. When a body moves to and fro about its mean position then this type of motion is knownas vibratory motion. The location of an object or a point or a place with respect to some reference point called origin is called its position. The length of actual path followed between two points is called the distance between these points. Displacement is the shortest distance from initial to final point which has magnitude and direction. The distance covered by a body in unit time is called speed. A body has uniform speed if it covers equal distance in equal intervals of time, however small these intervals of time may be. Greater is the mass of an object, more is the quantity of matter in it. The SI unit of mass is kilogram (kg). It is represented by symbol 'm’. In this universe, there are objects which cover a wide range of values of mass as shown in Table 4.1. If an object is at rest, then a force is needed to move it. The greater is the mass, the greater will be the force needed to move it. The reluctance or opposition offered by a mass whenever we try to change its state from rest to motion is called its inertia. In a similar way, a force is needed to stop a moving object. Passengers in a car have a lot of inertia so that they need seat-belts for their safety. If the car stops suddenly, the passengers in the car will tend to keep on moving unless the seat belts exert large forces to stop them. Thus, inertia is a property of matter by which it resists any change in its state of rest or uniform motion. 4.1.2 Measurement of Mass Mass of an object can be

text: Unit 4: Dynamics and Forces Physics IX A force may not always cause a body to move. e.g., if you push a wall, it is not possible to move it. However, the wall can be moved by applying a large force such as the force of a bulldozer. Thus, we can define the force as under. “A force produces or tends to produce motion in a body which is initially at rest; stops or tends to stop the moving body. It can change the speed of moving object. The force can also change the direction of motion of a body. It can also change the size or shape of an object" Force is a vector quantity. The resultant of two or more forces can be determined using the laws of vector addition. If two or more forces are acting along the same line and in same direction then the magnitude of the resultant force is equal to the sum of magnitudes of given forces. The direction of the resultant force will be same as that of given forces. 4.3 TYPES OF FORCES The forces are broadly classified into following two types. text: Unit 4: Dynamics and Forces Physics IX The force between two magnetic poles is called magnetic force. It is an established fact that like pole repel each other and unlike poles attract each other. A moving charge or current passing through a conductor sets up a magnetic field around it. Generally, the electric and magnetic effects cannot be separated for the case of a moving charge. When a charged particle is allowed to move in a magnetic field then a force acts on it. Thus this electromagnetic force is a combination of electric and magnetic forces. The gravitational and electromagnetic forces both are inversely proportional to the square of the separation between objects or charges. Thus, they decrease as the separation increases. However, the electromagnetic force is very strong as compared to gravitational force. For example, the force of electrostatic repulsion between two alpha particles separated by a distance of 10 m is about 3 x 10” times greater than the gravitational force between them. Thus, we are justified to say that gravitational force is almost negligible as compared with electrostatic force. The electromagnetic force is a long-range force. (iii) Strong Nuclear

text: Chapter 5: Momentum Physics IX 5.1 MOMENTUM By momentum (more precisely linear momentum) we mean as the “quantity of motion in an object”. All objects have mass so if an object is moving, then it has momentum because it has its mass in motion. Thus, the momentum of an object depends on its mass and velocity. A bullet has a very small mass but its impact is so strong, when it is fired from a gun because of its very high speed. On the other hand, the impact of a loaded truck ona body coming in its way is very large even if the truck is moving slowly because of its large mass. Thus, one can conclude that 'quantity of motion’ in an object depends on its mass and velocity. In terms of an equation, the momentum of an object is equal to the product of its mass and velocity. Momentum = Mass x Velocity p=mv (5.1) Momentum p is a vector quantity and its direction will be same as the direction of motion of object. An object at rest will have zero momentum because its velocity is zero. We can conclude from Eq. text: 8.2 ENERGY Energy is very important concept and frequently used in all sciences. We encounter it quite often in our daily life. We use our muscular energy to perform various activities of life i.e., breathing, talking, walking and running etc. We have to eat food on regular basis to sustain our muscular energy. The compressed spring of toy car has energy stored in it and enables the car to move. Similarly, the running water of a stream or river has energy. Man has been using this energy for centuries to grind food grains in water mill. Almost all natural phenomena are related to energy and its change. The energy of an object is defined as its capacity to do work. Energy is a scalar quantity and measured in joules. Energy exists in a variety of different forms. The various forms of energy include mechanical energy, chemical energy, thermal energy, solar energy, sound energy, electrical energy, magnetic energy and nuclear energy etc. 8.2.1 Forms of Energy Mechanical Energy It is the energy possessed by an object due to its position (i.e., potential energy) or due to its motion (i.e., kinetic energy). An object located at a height, compressed or stretched spring, a stretched bow and

An object located at a height, compressed or stretched spring, a stretched bow and water stored in a dam at an altitude etc. are examples of potential energy. Similarly, a moving cricket ball, a moving vehicle, moving water in a stream or river and wind are examples of kinetic energy. Fig.8. ‘xamples of mechanical energy Thermal Energy Thermal or heat energy is a form of energy associated with the motion of atoms or molecules of an object. Thermal energy is released from hot objects and flows from region of high temperature to region of low temperature. Sun is the main source of thermal energy. A large amount of thermal energy is released when fossil fuels like wood, coal, oil and natural gas etc. are burned [Figure 8.6]. We cook our

The frictional forces oppose the movement of objects and due to friction thermal energy is dissipated. Fig.8.6: Examples of thermal energy. Sound Energy Sound is a form of energy which is produced by the vibration of particles in a solid, liquid or gas. Sound energy is quite weak as compared with other forms of energy. However, humans and other animals are able to detect sound energy due to the special structure of their ears. Sound energy travels in a medium such as air, water and iron etc. in the form of waves but cannot travel in vacuum. We do not hear the sound of continued explosions taking place on Sun because sound waves cannot travel through vacuum. When you knock at the door, sound is produced. Beating of drum and loudspeaker are examples of production of sound energy [Figure 8.7]. Fig.8.7: Examples of sources of sound energy. In case of liquids, the charge carriers are positive and negative ions. Electrical energy

A stone held at certain altitude possess only gravitational potential energy. Whenit is allowed to fall freely then it starts moving towards the ground. Its gravitational potential energy starts converting into kinetic energy. By the time it hits the ground, all of its gravitational energy is converted into kinetic energy. Here we have assumed that loss of energy due to frictional forces is negligible. In case of simple pendulum, the total energy of the system keeps on changing between its kinetic energy and potential energy. It may be emphasized that there is always loss of energy whenever energy changes take place in real life.

Disadvantages of Hydroelectric Resources The following are the disadvantages of hydroelectric resources. (a) A large land area is required for dam. The energy of an object is defined as its capacity to do work. Mechanical energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its position (i.e., potential energy) or due to its motion (i.e., kinetic energy). Thermal or heat energy is a form of energy associated with the motion of atoms or molecules of an object. Sound is a form of energy which is produced by the vibration of particles in a solid, liquid or gas. Sound energy is quite weak as compared with other forms of energy. Electrical energy is due to flow of charged particles through a conductor. Chemical energy is the energy stored in the bonds of atoms and molecules of a substance. In fission process the nucleus of a heavy element splits into two light nuclei of nearly equal mass with release of a large amount of energy. Radiant or electromagnetic energy is the energy of electromagnetic waves. The examples of electromagnetic waves include gamma rays, Xrays, ultraviolet radiation, visible light, infrared radiation, radio waves and microwaves etc. The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor be destroyed but it can be transformed from one form to another. The energy possessed by an object due to its height from surface of Earth i.e., altitude is called gravitational potential energy. One or more atoms of same or different elements combine to form a molecule. Matter exists in three states i.e., solid, liquid and gas. Matter can change its state on heating or cooling. For example, ice (the solid form of water) will convert into liquid form i.e., water on heating. Further heating of water will convert it into steam which is the gaseous form of water. Similarly, the gaseous form of water i.e., steam can be transformed into its liquid form on cooling. Further cooling will transform the water into its solid form ice. Pressure can also change the state of matter. Gases can be liquified under high pressure. The existence of matter i.e., solid, liquid and gas may be explained on the basis of

The existence of matter i.e., solid, liquid and gas may be explained on the basis of the particle theory of matter. 12.2, PARTICLE THEORY OF MATTER The particle theory of matter is based on the following postulates. (a) Matter consists of extremely small particles. These particles are atoms, molecules or ions. (b) Particles are in constant motion and thus possess kinetic energy. The motion of particles can be translational, vibrational or rotational or a combination of these motions or all of these. The nature of motion of particles depends on the state of matter. (c) The particles of matter attract each other and this force depends on the separation between the particles. Smaller the separation between the particles, the greater will be the force of attraction between them. 12.3, SOLID, LIQUID AND GAS The different states of matter can be explained on the basis of particle theory of matter. The particles can vibrate only about their equilibrium position and cannot make any translation or rotation. Thus, the particles of a solid possess only vibrational kinetic energy. A solid has a definite shape and volume. The arrangement of particles in a solid is shown in Figure 12.1. Liquid When a solid is heated then it melts to change into its liquid form. On heating, the binding force between particles of solid becomes slightly weak. In a liquid, the separation between two particles is large as compared to that of a solid and for this reason density of most of liquids except mercury is less than that of solids. The particles of a liquid are arranged randomly and they can move freely from one to another part of liquid but are confined to the boundary ofcontainer. A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape. A liquid acquires the shape of its container. In other words, a liquid can flow. Gas The separation between the particles of a gas is very large as compared to the size of the particle This property results in extremely low value of density of gases as compared with solids and liquids. The forces of attraction between the particles of a gas are negligible due to their large separation distance The particles of gas are free to move randomly and in all directions within the boundary of container. The particles of gas move at high speeds and may spin at elevated temperature. Thus, a gas can possess translational, vibrational and _ rotational kinetic energies depending upon its temperature. text: INTRODUCTION Among the creatures, human being is the only creature who has ability of thinking, reasoning and researching. On account of this ability, he is trying to gain knowledge about the origin, creation and organization of this vast universe and the different related laws governing it. He also endeavours to explain the hidden natural reservoirs and forces (acting and reacting) which cause various events in the universe. In the past, man was reluctant to think about the universe but at present, he wishes to make an abode on moon or on any other planet. Quantization rules of electrons in an atom, a solar system and a massive body like galaxy all these have become part of the study and observation of the mankind. Similarly, a man researches to reason out that how the life of living things (plants and animals) get possibility to exist and evaluate only on earth? How days and nights are formed by the spin motion of the earth? How changing of seasons aré timed by orbital motion of the earth? In the same way, how the process of evapotization, condensation and sterilization take place? In short, the knowledge,about the nature in terms of research, observations and practical

In short, the knowledge,about the nature in terms of research, observations and practical applications.are known as science. Gradually, due to rapid research, the volume of knowledge‘about science increases. Therefore, science is basically classified into two maincclasses; Biological sciences which deals with study of living things and Physical sciences which deals with study of non- living things. Physical sciences can bé.further sub divided into five main branches ie.; Chemistry, Geology, Astronomy; Meteorology and Physics. The word Physics comes from the Greek word ‘Physis’ Physika or Physikos meaning the knowledge of the nature and natural world, On the other hand, Physics is the study of properties of matter and energy and the mutual relationship ‘between them. text: 1.6 SIGNIFICANT FIGURES | The number of accurately known digits and the first doubtful digit are called significant figures. It is explained as; The measurement of physical quantities made by related instruments often involves some errors or uncertainties. These uncertaintics are due to the following factors: (i) The least count of measuring instruments (ii) Quality and condition of the apparatus (iii) Skill of the observer (iv) Different recorded observations by the same apparatus. In the presence of these complications, the reported result centains both certain and uncertain digits and the total number of all these certain and uncertain digits are known as significant figures. For example, let the reported mass of a sphere is 1.53°kg. In this case 1 and 5 are certain digits while 3 is uncertain and the measured yalue has three significant figures. Similarly, the reported length of a simple pendulum is 102.5 cm, this value has four significant figures, the digits 1, 0 and 2 are certain while 5 is uncertain. 1.6.1 Rules for determining the numberof significant figures The number of significant figure of a measured value can be determined ° under the following rules. text: These uncertainties are called errors and these are due to the following factors. (a) Zero error and faulty or poor condition of the instrument. (b) Irrelevant experimental technique or procedure. (c) Lack of experience in the setting and using of the apparatus. (d) Taking observation without precautions. The error in the measurement can be minimized by using the instrument which contains small uncertainty. For example, between metre rod and vernier callipers, the measurement by using vernier callipers is more reliable than metre rod, because it has small uncertainty. The errors in measurement can be classified into two main classes. (i) Systematic Error (ii) Random Error 1.7.1 Systematic Errors ° The errors that appear in measurement and repeat in Same magnitude and sign under the same conditions are called systematic errors, Such errors are due to the following factors i.e., the zero error in instrument, poor calibration of instrument and incorrect marking. : Systematic error can be removed by using some standard instruments. 1.7.2 Random Errors The errors that appear in measurement and repeat in different magnitude and sign under the same conditions are called random errors.

Significant Figures: A reported result by an observer always contain both certain and uncertain digits. The number of these certain digits and first uncertain digit are known as significant figures. Random Error: The errors which appear in measurement due to unknown causes are known as random errors. These errors repeat in different magnitudes and signs. text: INTRODUCTION on that all bodies are either at rest or in motion. A body is said to be at rest if it does not change its position with respect to its surroundings. For example, a book placed on a table. "A body is said to be in motion, if it changes its position with respect to its surroundings". For example, a man, walking a moving car or a train etc. In universe, everything is in perpetual motion, like motion of ap electron around the nucleus, the motion of the moon around the earth, earth moves around the sun and so many others. The motion can be categorized into three types i.c., translational, rotational and vibrational. For example, motion of a car along a highway is a translational motion)motion of fan is a rotational motion and to and fro motion of a pendulum is a vibrational motion. All kinds of motion can be explained in terms of displacement, velocity, acceleration and force. These parameters can be studied in the equations of motion and Newton’s three laws of motion. text: [EE . Inelastic Collision A collision in which the linear momentum of a body is conserved, but total energy is not conserved is called inelastic collision. The experiment shows that there is loss in kinetic energy in inelastic collision. This loss of energy appears in the other forms of energy, such as heat, sound etc. For example, when a bouncing ball is dropped on to a hard floor, the collision between the ball and floor is elastic and the ball would not lose its kinetic energy and so would rebound to its original height. However practically, the actual rebound height is slightly shorter, showing some loss of kinetic energy in collision. Such collision is called inelastic collision. Simiiarly, the collision between cars, mud thrown on the wall and'sticking to it and the collision between bullet and its target are the examples of inelastic collision: During inelastic collision kinetic energy is not conserved, it is converted into various forms especially heat and sound. INTRODUCTION Wosk and energy are not two different things, but they are correlated to each other. When work is done by one system on another, indeed energy is transferred between the two systems. For example, when an engine pulls a train along a horizontal track, the engine does work. The engine transfers energy. to the train. If we assume that there is no loss of energy, then the amount of energy of the moving train is equal to the work done. Similarly, when we walk upstairs, we do work; our work is equal to gain in gravitational Potential Energy (P.E). Energy is present in the universe in various forms. It'can be converted from one form into other form but neither be created nor be destroyed. This is the principle of conservation of energy. For example, a heat engine tonverts heat energy into mechanical energy. A fan converts electrical'energy into mechanical energy, a bulb

A fan converts electrical'energy into mechanical energy, a bulb converts electrical energy into light and-heat energy etc. All forms of energy can be explained in terms of kinetic energy or potential energy. These two are the most important types of energies. The Kinetic Energy (K.E) is due to motion while P.E is a stored energy. Here a question arises, how much work is done or how much energy is consumed? It is measured in terms of rate of doing work or rate of consumption of energy which is called power. For example, a boy may carry a box upstairs in 3 minutes while a man may. do it in 1 minute. Obviously, the power of the man is more than the’power of the boy. Thus, time factor is important for power. A body which has the capacity to do work is said to possess energy. The greater the capacity of the body to do.work, the greater is the energy possessed by it. Thus work, energy and power are related.to each other. It is possible only when a system or a device is free from friction. In real life situation, frictional forces are always present and a device cannot do any work without friction. Due to presence of frictional forces, it is not possible to convert the available energy completely into useful work. Only a fraction of energy is converted into useful work and the rest is wasted in form of heat. How much energy is utilized for the useful work by the system or device and how much energy is wasted? text: INTRODUCTION Basically, there are three states of matter namely solid, liquid and gas. Each State has different nature on the basis of its different properties. For example, the atoms in liquids and gases are not closely bounded but they are at some distance. Typically, the distance between two molecules of liquid is 107 m and the distance between molecules of the gases is 10°! m. Due to this large space between molecules of liquid and gases, they have the ability to flow under the influence of some applied forces and hence they are called fluid. A liquid flows and acquires the shape of the container. A gas also flows into a container and spreads out until it occupies the entire volume of the container. . Moreover, the distance between the molecules of gas is more than the liquids, so a gas can be compressed while the compression of liquid isyalmost negligible. Fluid plays a vital role in many aspect of our everyday life. For example, we drink them, breath them, swim in them, they circulate through our bodies, airplanes fly through them, ships float in them. text: Sphygmomanometer It is a device used to measure the blood’ pressure. The schematic diagram of Sphygmomanometer is shown in Fig. 6.16. It consists of an inflatable rubber cuff, which is wrapped around the arm of the person and a manometer is also attached with it. When the external pressure is increased beyond the systolic pressure by pumping the rubber ball, then a force is exerted on the cuff such that the arm is squeezed and flow of blood through arteries is stopped. When the external pressure becomes equal to the systolic ‘pressure, then the velocity of the blood becomes high and turbulent. The external pressure is further decreased such that its value becomes equal to the diastolic pressure. At this point, the arteries are relaxed. text: 7.7 DAMPED OSCILLATION In free oscillation, we have studied that the total mechanical energy of the oscillating body remains constant. But in practices, when a body is oscillating with its natural frequency, the amplitude of the oscillation gradually decreases with time and finally it comes to rest. This is due to the presence of resistive forces such as; air resistance, friction etc. The oscillation with decreasing amplitude in the presence of various - resistive forces is called damped oscillation and the resistive forces are called damping. forces. Energy dissipates due to negative work done by these damping forces - and the body comes to rest in due course of time. The damping force depends upon the speed of the oscillating body and is directed opposite to the velocity. Graphically the damped oscillation of the oscillating ney is shown in Fig. 7.15. ‘ . text: Examples of damping devices shock absorber ° In damped oscillation, a small fraction of gy of the oscillating system is dissipated against the friction but damping in some cases is very useful. One widely used application of damped oscillation is in the suspension system of aii automobile. A shock absorber is attached to the frame of the vehicle. the ener; A shock absorber is designed to use damping forces, which reduce the vibrations related with a bumpy ride. As Fig.7.19 shows, a shock absorber consists of a piston in a reservoir of viscous fluid such as oil. When the piston moves up and down in response to a bump on the road, the oil inside the pressure tube is forced to go through piston valve and the base valve to move into thé adjacent chamber. The holes in the valve control the rate of oil flow. Viscous forces that arise during this movement cause the damping effect. The idea behind a shock absorber is to ease the natural bouncing motion.of a spring. The degree of damping of shock absorber is shown in Fig.7.20. text: 7.8 FORCED OSCILLATION AND RESONANCE In damped osciflation, the oscillator cannot maintain its natural frequency for long duration due to the resistive forces and the amplitude of the oscillation decreases gradually with time. But we can maintain constant amplitude by applying a periodic extemal force which is called a driving force. Thus when the oscillating body is subjected to a periodic driving force then such oscillation is called ‘ forced oscillation and its frequency is called driving frequency. text: INTRODUCTION The properties and the nature of light was studied by many scientists based on different theories but two of them were commendable, that is Newton’s corpuscular theory and Christian Huygen's wave theory. Newton believed that light consists of smail particles called corpuscles and he was successful in reflection and refraction phenomenons. There are two experiments photoelectric effect and Compton’s effect which have been verified the Newton’s corpuscular theory and these will be studied in Modern physics in the next class. In 1676, Huygens explained the light in terms of wave. According to this wave theory, light és travelling in the form of a wave. The wave theory ‘ean explain reflection, refraction and the phenomenon of double refraction. The Huygen’s wave theory of light was not acceptable by Newton and others. Because the knowledge of waves was confined to mechanical waves only and it requires some medium for its propagation and there was no idea about electromagnetic waves. Therefore, Huygen proposed hypothetical medium Ether. One important.difference between the two theories was that the corpuscular theory predicted that light would travel faster in a material

One important.difference between the two theories was that the corpuscular theory predicted that light would travel faster in a material medium than air, whereas the wave theory predicted a slower velocity in a dense medium. Later on, it was proved experimentally that the velocity of light is faster in rare medium. Similarly, James Clark Maxwell presented the idea of electromagnetic waves. Electromagnetic waves can propagate through vacuum. It has same properties as that of the light and the speed of thiswave is equal to speed of light i.e. 3x10°ms'. Thus, Maxwell concluded that light waves are electromagnetic waves and.require no :- medium suchas ether for their propagation. In 1801, Young provided an experimental proof of wave theory of light by performing interference,of light. Similarly, the result of diffraction is also a strong evidence of the wave:theory of light.
